messages.content: Write a customer case study about a company that adopted a continuous delivery platform and now deploys more often. Around 250 words.

output:
Fictional company — I don't have a real customer to write about, so this is an illustrative example. Swap in the real names and numbers, or tell me the actual account and I'll redo it.

---

**Kestrel Freight: from a three-week release train to 61 deploys a week**

Kestrel Freight builds routing software for European trucking fleets: 240 engineers, one large Java monolith, and until last March, a release that shipped every third Wednesday.

The Wednesday was the problem. Miss it and your change sat for three weeks, quietly rotting next to forty other people's changes. By release day the diff was 900 commits deep. When something broke, and something usually did, nobody could say which commit broke it. "We spent more time bisecting than building," says Marta Oyelaran, who runs platform engineering there.

Kestrel moved to the platform in stages over five months. Trunk-based branching first, then the deployment pipeline, then progressive rollout by fleet region. The monolith stayed a monolith. That was deliberate; splitting it would have added a year to the project.

Numbers after eight months:

- Commit to production, median: 11 days → 1 hour 40 minutes
- Deploys per week: 0.3 → 61
- Change failure rate: 18% → 4%
- Mean time to restore: 6 hours → 12 minutes

The failure-rate drop surprised them. Smaller changes are easier to reason about, and a bad deploy now reverts on its own when error rates cross the canary threshold.

It has not all been smooth. Test flakiness that the three-week cadence had hidden turned into a daily irritation, and Kestrel spent two months quarantining and rewriting about 400 integration tests before the pipeline was trustworthy. Oyelaran calls that work the real migration.

Kestrel now ships on Fridays. That, they say, is the part the team still finds strange.
